div.p: A systems architecture is presented that will guarantee crucial timing requirements, is tolerant of a range of hardware errors, but is sufficiently flexible for sporadic activities to be guaranteed and non-real-time tasks to be accommodated. The model presented uses static allocation of application tasks, preemptive priority based scheduling, and replication for task availability.

div.head: INTRODUCTION
div.p: This paper presents a systems architecture that is aimed at providing a flexible environment for applications, and which is both real-time and tolerant of a range of hardware faults. The architecture proposed has been obtained by choosing (known) fault tolerant techniques that are amenable to timing analysis, extending schedulability models to incorporate these techniques, and using, to advantage, properties of the computational model usually applied in hard real-time applications.

The unification of real-time and fault tolerance in a single systems architecture has two ramifications in terms of error treatment: 0 there are a class of errors due to timing faults (e.g. deadlines being missed), and 0 error recovery has a timing requirement. The magnitude of the deadline on error recovery varies greatly between application domains; and can give rise to quite different architectures. For example on an unmanned satellite a completely cold restart is adequate. At the other extreme many avionic systems require completely undisturbed availability through many classes of failure. In the work presented here we attempt to support the latter type of requirement where there is a need for the execution environment to continue to deliver a service in the presence of hardware failures.

div.head: Basic Hardware Architecture
div.p: We focus on distributed systems in which one or more processors form nodes that are linked to a broadcast LAN via a network connector. From a timing perspective there are thus four main issues: 1.
It follows that from a safety critical stand point a distributed system must be tolerant of node failure, message loss and network connector failure.

The allocation of computational activities to nodes. The management of each node (i.e. the order in which computations are carried out). The management on the communications media (i.e. the order in which messages are sent). The management of the information exchange between each node and its network connector.

div.head: Computational Model
div.p: An application is assumed to consists of a fixed collection of precedence related tasks. Tasks may preempt one another and may pass information asynchronously using protected data that imposes mutual exclusion. Timing requirements are usually assigned to rrunsucrions running through a number of tasks from an input (or timing) event to an output activity. We distinguish, and wish to support, periodic transactions and sporadic transactions. This will enable applications to have both event mggered and time mggered processing.

The computational model implicit in this paper has the following properties: It consists of active entities (tasks) and protected shared data areas. The only communication between active entities is via the shared data areas; the only exception to this is when one active entity releases another for execution. Precedence relationships between active entities are allowed. Active entities have temporal attributes defined (such as deadline, offset, period, minimal arrival rate etc). Shared data areas provide mutual exclusion but do not arbitrarily block clients. Entities are allocated (statically) to single processing units.

The allowable remote actions (in the distributed system) are a remote write to an external shared data area, and the releasing of a remote active entity. This simple model has sufficiently expressive power to allow systems to be designed, allocated to distributed hardware, and analysed for realistic worst case behaviour. For example the following three development methods embody this model: (a) MASCOea traditional approach (b) TAM16a formal method (c) HRT-HOOD9 -An object oriented approach 0 1.3. Requirements of the Systems Architecture Our perspective on the problems involved in building safety-critical real-time systems leads to the following basic requirements: simplicity: (provable) run-time techniques such as static preemptive priority based scheduling; predictability: 100% guarantees on the timing behaviour of all crucial computations (within some failure hypothesis); reliability: coverage of realistic failure possibilities in the failure hypothesis; flexibility: to facilitate the effective use of spare resources generated at run-time, the incorporation of sporadic (non-deterministic) activities, and soft real-time (or background) computations; maintainability: incorporation of change management to facilitate the evolutionary change to a non-stop long-life system. 0

div.head: GUARANTEEING THE REAL-TIME PROPERTIES
div.p: Scheduling the Nodes Choosing a paradigm for scheduling is difficult due to the apparent contradiction between the needs for flexibility and predictability. MARS'O uses a cyclic scheduling approach in order to have complete predictability as to when the computational events occur. This approach however makes it very difficult to incorporate sporadic activities. At the other extreme the use of udlity (or best effort) based scheduling14 gives great flexibility but does not, in its general form, allow loo% guarantees to be constructed. We believe that process based preemptive priority ordered dispatching gives the basis for flexibility whilst allowing guarantees to be made. The rate monotonic theory has had considerable success in this area. Here priorities are essentially static, apart from the use of inheritance during task interactions1'. For example, the protected data used for asynchronous communication can have their mutual exclusion requirement satisfied by assigning a ceiling priority to the dataeach user task has its priority raised to the ceiling level when it is interacting with the resource.

Whilst the rate monotonic scheme requires task period to be equal to its deadline, the scheduling (and allocation) of transactions requires this resmction to be removed. Recently schedulability tests for more flexible behaviour have been derived. This allows a wide range of application requirements to be satisfied. For example: deadlines less than period4, sporadic tasks2, release 'itter and non-regular periodicity5, arbitrary deadlines (i.e. deadlines greater than ~e r i o d ) ~~. ~~, and offsets (i.e. not all tasks sharing a critical i n ~t a n c e ) l . ~~* ~. These tests can be used to guarantee periodic and sporadic transactions. The intermediate deadlines of the tasks involved in the transaction are chosen as part of the allocation process. Allocation is necessarily entwined with node scheduling. We have used the technique of simulated annealing to produce feasible allocations for distributed real-time systems21. 8.

div.head: Scheduling the LAN
div.p: There are also a number of techniques available for managing the LAN. The most flexible allows open access and contends with collisions when they occur13; the most predicatable uses TDh4A'o.12 to preallocate all messages. Again there is a need to choose the most flexible approach on which guarantees can be built. Two methods are possible: 0 0 A global priority protocol'8. In the former method nodes can only broadcast when they hold the token; the token progresses around the network in a fixed and known order. Messages are sent in a priority order from each node. As part of the allocation activity, the maximum holding time for each node (and hence token rotation time) is calculated. In general a message from one task to a remote successor (in some transaction) is transmitted when the node next has the token. If a node has no messages to transmit then the token can be passed on early (although we shall see that there is a constraint on this). Priority based scheduling is optimal but requires more sophisticated support from the hardware.

div.head: Scheduling the Network Connector
div.p: A key aspect of the communications facility is the method used to move incoming data from the network buffer to memory that the application tasks running on the host node can access. This has not received as much attention in the literature as other aspects of communication.

The standard non-real-time LAN connector uses DMA for the data transfer; but this is unpredictable for real-time systems as short periods of over 90% cycle stealing can be e ~p e r i e n c e d ~~. For a fully predictable architecture his data transfer must be scheduled with the rest of the system. One approach, which we have described elsewhere', is to use dual port memory (between the connector and the host) and to schedule the communications work as a sporadic task on the host (this task typically has deadline greater than period). As the maximum number of messages each node can receive is known (a priori), the buffer size (on this dual port memory) can be made adequate. When the message arrives the network connector generates an interrupt into the host which activates a sporadic task which then manages the movement of the data from the buffer to the areas needed for the receiving tasks.

The execution time of this task is known (as the maximum number of messages is known). It is synchronised to the arrival of the message, so the end-to-end message delay can be calculated. Furthermore the impact on the host processor of running the sporadic server is amenable to analyses using the normal scheduling tests.

One problem however remains: if the network at some time is lightly loaded the token will rotate very fast and hence generate two "token arrived interrupts" close together. If the sporadic task was designed to accommodate this, it would impose a heavy and pessimistic load on the host. Hence it is necessary to impose a minimum rotation time on the token; a node cannot pass on the token to its successor until a specified time interval (measured locally) has elapsed since it last passed it on. The time interval is again chosen as part of the allocation activity.

div.head: Tolerating Failures
div.p: A safety critical architecture must be tolerant of some known failure modes. Message loss, or corruption, is to be expected and hence must be accommodated in the scheduling model. A certain level of re-broadcasting can be anticipated and allowed for. Node failure is usually dealt with by replicating the critical tasks on different nodes. The LAN must then provide an atomic broadcast. The timed token passing protocol is easily extended to give this provision. The global priority scheme requires further analysis. Considerable benefit accrues from making the network connector fail silent. This is done in the Delta-4 project15.

div.head: CONCLUSIONS
div.p: The above has presented an informal description of an architecture aimed at providing useful fault coverage and real-time behaviour. The description could not be exhaustive and a number of specific issues were not addressed. Nevertheless sufficient details, and motivations, are given for an assessment to be made. The overall goal of the design is to provide a systems architecture model that will guarantee 100% all crucial computations within a stated failure hypothesis. Moreover the faults covered by this hypothesis are deemed to be ones of practical importance.
